impact_quest.description: Your research proves urban green spaces reduce anxiety in deprived neighbourhoods. The paper is published, now can you turn it into real-world change before REF 2029?

animal_hoarding.title: The Hoarding Gap
animal_hoarding.description: The UK has no legal definition of animal hoarding. Your research could change that, if you can navigate the right stakeholders.

bfr.title: From Clinic to Cosmos
bfr.description: Your Blood Flow Restriction research works in rehab clinics. Now NASA and ESA want it for space. Can you scale from lab to orbit?

sbl.title: The Simulation Lab
sbl.description: One-third of teachers leave within five years. Can simulation-based learning transform how we prepare them for the classroom?

start.title: The Impact Quest
start.narrative:
You're a researcher at a UK university. Your team has just published a ground breaking study on how community-led urban green spaces reduce anxiety and improve social cohesion in deprived neighbourhoods.

The paper is strong and is published in a top journal with robust methodology. But right now, it's just words on a page. Your Head of School has flagged your work as having impact potential and the university's Impact Officer has reached out.

The clock is ticking toward REF 2029. What you do next will determine whether this research changes lives, or gathers dust.

choices.text: Meet with your Impact Officer to develop a strategy
Go straight to social media and start promoting the paper
Contact the local council directly, they need to hear this straight away

meet_officer.title: Strategic Thinking
meet_officer.narrative:
Smart move. Your Impact Officer is enthusiastic. At your next meeting they help you map out a Theory of Change, connecting your research findings to potential real-world outcomes.

"We need to think about WHO could use this research, HOW they'd use it, and what EVIDENCE we'd need to prove it made a difference."

Together you identify three potential impact pathways:
- Policy influence: informing local or national green space policy
- Practitioner change: helping community organisations design better programmes
- Public benefit: directly improving wellbeing in target communities

Which pathway do you want to prioritise first?

choices.text: Policy influence: let's aim high and target policymakers
Practitioner change: let's work with community organisations on the ground
Can we pursue all three at once?

social_media_first.title: Going Viral (Sort Of)
social_media_first.narrative:
You write a LinkedIn post about your research. It gets 200 likes, a few reshares from other academics, and one reply from someone saying "this is obvious."

A journalist from a regional paper picks it up and writes a short piece: "University boffins discover parks are good for you." It's not exactly the nuanced coverage you hoped for.

The reach is broad but shallow. You've raised awareness, but awareness alone isn't impact, at least not the kind REF panels are looking for. You need to show your research actually CHANGED something.

Your Impact Officer sends you a gentle email: "Great to see the media coverage! Shall we meet to discuss turning this attention into something more strategic?"

choices.text: Take your Impact Officer up on the offer, it's time to get strategic
Double down on media and pitch to national outlets
A community group has commented on the article. Reach out to them

cold_call_council.title: The Cold Shoulder
cold_call_council.narrative:
You email the local council's environment team with your paper attached and a note saying "This could transform your green space strategy!"

Three weeks pass. Nothing.

You follow up. A junior officer replies: "Thanks for sending this. We'll keep it on file." That's council-speak for the recycling bin.

The problem? You approached them without understanding their priorities, timelines, or how they actually make decisions. Policy engagement is a different skill from academic publishing.

Your colleague mentions that the university has a Policy Engagement training session next month, run by the Impact and Engagement team.

choices.text: Attend the policy engagement training
Try a different approach  -  find a personal connection at the council
Forget the council  -  focus on community organisations instead

meet_officer_late.title: Better Late Than Never
meet_officer_late.narrative:
Sam doesn't judge. "The media coverage actually gives us something to work with," they say. "But we need to move from awareness to action."

Sam helps you develop a stakeholder map and a proper engagement plan. You identify that your research is most relevant to:

* The council's Public Health team (not Environment  -  they don't have budget)
* Three local community organisations already running green space projects
* A national charity that funds urban greening initiatives

"The key," Sam says, "is to listen first. Find out what THEY need, then show how your research helps."

choices.text: Start with the community organisations  -  build from the ground up
Target the national charity  -  they could fund a bigger project

media_blitz.title: Diminishing Returns
media_blitz.narrative:
You pitch to The Guardian, BBC, and several national outlets. One radio station invites you for a 3-minute interview at 6:40am. You do it half-asleep and stumble over the key findings.

A few more articles appear, but they all say roughly the same thing. Your university's comms team is pleased, but when you talk to Sam the Impact Officer, they're candid:

"Media coverage is great for public engagement, but REF panels want to see your research actually changed behaviour, practice, or policy. A newspaper article isn't evidence of impact  -  it's evidence of dissemination."

This lands hard. You've been busy, but have you been effective?

choices.text: Regroup with Sam and build a proper impact strategy
A council officer saw the BBC piece and got in touch  -  follow up

community_contact.title: A Grassroots Connection
community_contact.narrative:
The community group  -  GreenSpace Collective  -  runs urban gardens in three deprived wards. Their coordinator, Priya, is excited about your research.

"We've been telling the council for years that our gardens help people's mental health, but we never had the evidence. Your study could change everything for us."

Priya invites you to visit their sites and meet participants. You spend a Saturday morning pulling weeds and chatting to people whose lives have been genuinely transformed by the green spaces.

This is powerful. But how do you turn a Saturday morning into REF-quality impact?

choices.text: Co-design a wellbeing measurement tool with GreenSpace Collective
Help them write a funding bid using your research evidence
Invite Priya to give a guest lecture at the university

policy_route.title: The Policy Pathway
policy_route.narrative:
Sam connects you with the university's Policy Engagement lead, who helps you craft a policy brief  -  a concise, jargon-free summary of your findings with clear recommendations.

You learn that effective policy engagement means:
* Understanding the policy cycle and timing your interventions
* Speaking their language, not yours
* Offering solutions, not just findings
* Building relationships over time, not just sending documents

The policy brief is excellent. Now you need to get it in front of the right people. The local council is refreshing its Health & Wellbeing Strategy, and there's a public consultation opening next month.

choices.text: Submit a formal response to the consultation using your evidence
Request a meeting with the Director of Public Health
Both  -  submit the response AND request the meeting

practitioner_route.title: Working With Communities
practitioner_route.narrative:
You connect with three community organisations running green space projects across the region. Each has different needs:

* GreenSpace Collective wants evidence to support their funding bids
* Park Life CIC wants to redesign their programme based on what actually works
* The Neighbourhood Trust wants to train volunteers using evidence-based approaches

All three are enthusiastic, but you're one person with a full teaching load and two PhD students to supervise. Sam warns: "Don't overcommit. One deep partnership beats three shallow ones for REF purposes."

choices.text: Go deep with GreenSpace Collective  -  co-produce new resources
Work with Park Life CIC to redesign their programme
Try to support all three  -  you can manage it

all_three.title: Ambition vs. Reality
all_three.narrative:
Sam pauses. "I love the ambition, but let me be honest  -  trying to do everything at once usually means nothing gets done well. REF panels can spot a mile-wide, inch-deep impact narrative immediately."

"The strongest impact case studies tell a focused story: clear pathway, strong evidence, demonstrable change. We can absolutely pursue multiple pathways eventually, but let's nail one first."

This is good advice. Which pathway has the most potential right now?

choices.text: Policy influence  -  there's a council consultation coming up
Practitioner change  -  community groups are already interested

policy_training.title: Learning the Craft
policy_training.narrative:
The policy engagement training is a revelation. You learn about:

* How policy is actually made (spoiler: it's messier than you thought)
* The difference between policy influence and policy change
* How to write a briefing note that a civil servant will actually read
* The importance of timing  -  policy windows open and close

Crucially, you learn that the council is about to refresh its Health & Wellbeing Strategy. There's a 12-week public consultation starting next month. This is your window.

You also meet a colleague from Public Health who has contacts in the council's wellbeing team.

choices.text: Prepare a formal consultation response with your evidence
Ask your Public Health colleague for an introduction to the council team

find_connection.title: The Warm Introduction
find_connection.narrative:
You mention your council frustrations at a faculty event, and a colleague in Public Health says: "Oh, you need to talk to Janet in the council's wellbeing team. We collaborated on a project last year. Let me introduce you."

This is how policy engagement actually works  -  through relationships and trust, not cold emails.

Janet agrees to a coffee meeting. She's frank: "We get dozens of research papers sent to us. What makes yours different is that you're here, asking what we need, rather than telling us what you've found."

Janet reveals that the council is developing a new Green Space Action Plan.

choices.text: Offer to present your findings to Janet's team
Ask Janet what evidence gaps the council has  -  tailor your input to their needs

warm_intro.title: The Warm Introduction
warm_intro.narrative:
Your colleague introduces you to Janet, a senior officer in the council's wellbeing team. Janet agrees to meet for coffee.

She's refreshingly direct: "Academics usually tell us what they've found and expect us to be grateful. What would actually help is if you could tell us what WORKS and for WHOM  -  in plain English, with costs."

She mentions the council is developing a new Green Space Action Plan and they're short on evidence about mental health outcomes.

choices.text: Offer to present your findings to Janet's team
Ask what specific evidence gaps the council needs filled

consultation.title: The Formal Response
consultation.narrative:
You submit a detailed, evidence-based response to the Health & Wellbeing Strategy consultation. It's well-crafted, citing your research and making clear, actionable recommendations about green space investment.

Two months later, the final strategy is published. Buried in the evidence annex, your paper is cited. One of your recommendations about "community-led green space programmes" appears in the action plan, though reworded.

This is genuine policy influence! But the evidence trail is thin  -  how do you prove your research specifically contributed to this change?

choices.text: Request a letter from the council acknowledging your research contribution
Write a follow-up FOI request to see how consultation responses were used
Meet with Janet at the council to discuss next steps and document the connection

consultation_and_meeting.title: Belt and Braces
consultation_and_meeting.narrative:
Excellent instinct. You submit the consultation response AND secure a meeting with the Director of Public Health (DPH).

The DPH is interested: "We know green spaces matter, but we've struggled to make the economic case. Can your research help us model the cost-benefit?"

This is a golden opportunity  -  but it's also scope creep. Cost-benefit analysis wasn't part of your original study. However, your colleague in Health Economics might be able to help.

Meanwhile, your consultation response is logged formally, creating a paper trail.

choices.text: Collaborate with Health Economics to produce the cost-benefit analysis
Stick to what your research actually shows  -  don't overreach

dph_meeting.title: Aiming High
dph_meeting.narrative:
Getting a meeting with the Director of Public Health takes some persistence, but your Impact Officer Sam uses a university contact to broker an introduction.

The DPH gives you 30 minutes. You present your findings clearly. They're engaged but pragmatic: "This is interesting, but I need to know: what would you recommend we actually DO differently based on this?"

This is the moment. Policy makers don't want data dumps  -  they want actionable recommendations.

choices.text: Recommend the council funds community-led green space programmes in deprived wards
Suggest a pilot project to test your approach in one neighbourhood first

codesign.title: Co-Production Gold
codesign.narrative:
You work with GreenSpace Collective over six months to co-design a wellbeing measurement toolkit. It's based on your research but shaped by the community's own language and priorities.

The toolkit is practical, accessible, and genuinely useful. GreenSpace Collective starts using it across their three sites. Other organisations hear about it and want copies.

Priya says: "For the first time, we can actually show funders what difference we make. This has transformed how we work."

This is strong impact evidence  -  practice change driven by your research. But you need to document it properly.

choices.text: Commission independent testimonials and a case study from GreenSpace Collective
Track the toolkit's adoption  -  how many organisations are using it?
Apply for follow-on funding to scale the toolkit nationally

programme_redesign.title: Evidence Into Practice
programme_redesign.narrative:
Park Life CIC works with you to redesign their community programme using your evidence. They restructure their sessions to include the elements your research identified as most beneficial: social connection time, nature contact, and participant-led activities.

After six months, their participant satisfaction scores increase significantly, and they report better mental health outcomes among attendees.

The CIC's director writes to you: "Your research has fundamentally changed how we deliver our programme. We're seeing real differences in people's lives."

choices.text: Document this with before/after data and testimonials
Help Park Life present this at a national community health conference

overcommit.title: Stretched Too Thin
overcommit.narrative:
You try to support all three organisations simultaneously. For two months, you're racing between meetings, missing deadlines, and sending rushed emails.

GreenSpace Collective's Priya sends a carefully worded message: "We really value the partnership, but we haven't seen the draft toolkit you promised in January. We need it for our March funding bid."

Park Life stops replying to your emails. The Neighbourhood Trust moves on and finds a consultant instead.

Sam checks in: "How's it going?" You're honest: it's not going well.

"It's not too late to refocus," Sam says. "Pick one and do it properly."

choices.text: Recommit to GreenSpace Collective  -  apologise and deliver
Reconnect with Park Life CIC  -  they had the clearest need

council_inbound.title: An Unexpected Ally
council_inbound.narrative:
A council officer named Janet saw your BBC interview and reaches out: "We're developing a new Green Space Action Plan and your research is exactly what we need. Could we meet?"

This is the dream scenario  -  a policy maker coming to YOU. But you need to handle it well. Janet's interest is genuine but time-limited; if you don't deliver value quickly, the moment will pass.

choices.text: Meet Janet immediately and ask what evidence she needs
Prepare a polished briefing document first, then meet

council_presentation.title: Making Your Case
council_presentation.narrative:
You present your findings to the council's wellbeing team. You've learned from earlier mistakes  -  no jargon, clear recommendations, costs and benefits laid out simply.

The team is engaged. Two things happen:

1. Your evidence is incorporated into the council's new Green Space Action Plan
2. Janet asks if you'd sit on an advisory panel for the plan's implementation

This is significant policy influence. Your research is directly shaping council strategy. But for REF purposes, you'll need written evidence of this influence.

choices.text: Accept the advisory role and request formal documentation of your contribution
Focus on getting a letter from the council confirming the research influence

needs_led.title: Listening First
needs_led.narrative:
You spend an hour listening to Janet describe the council's challenges. It turns out they need evidence on three things:

1. Which types of green space interventions are most cost-effective
2. How to target provision at communities with the greatest need
3. Whether community-led approaches work better than council-managed ones

Your research directly addresses points 2 and 3. Point 1 would need additional analysis, but your Health Economics colleague could help.

Janet is impressed that you asked rather than assumed. "This is how academics should work with us," she says.

choices.text: Produce a tailored evidence briefing addressing all three questions
Focus only on what your research covers (points 2 and 3)  -  stay credible

charity_route.title: Following the Money
charity_route.narrative:
You approach GreenFutures, a national charity that funds urban greening. Their research lead is interested in your work and invites you to present at their annual conference.

The conference goes well. GreenFutures asks if you'd co-develop an evidence framework for assessing community green space projects  -  essentially embedding your research into how they evaluate and fund programmes nationally.

This could mean your research influences dozens of projects across the country.

choices.text: Accept  -  this is national-scale impact
Accept, but also maintain the local community partnerships

funding_bid.title: Empowering Partners
funding_bid.narrative:
You help GreenSpace Collective write a funding bid to the National Lottery, using your research as the evidence base. The bid makes a compelling case: here's the research showing this approach works, and here's the community organisation ready to deliver it.

The bid is successful  -  ÃÂÃÂ£150,000 over three years. Priya is ecstatic. Your research has directly enabled this community organisation to expand their life-changing work.

This is tangible, evidenced impact. The funding decision letter explicitly cites your research as key supporting evidence.

choices.text: Document this carefully  -  the funding letter is gold-standard evidence
Negotiate a research partnership within the funded project

guest_lecture.title: Nice, But...
guest_lecture.narrative:
Priya gives a great guest lecture. Students love hearing from a practitioner. But Sam gently points out:

"A guest lecture is a lovely thing, but it's not really impact  -  it's just internal university activity. Impact means your research changed something OUT THERE in the world.

"Priya's visit is actually more valuable as a relationship-building step. What can you do WITH her organisation, not just have them talk TO your students?"

choices.text: You're right  -  let's co-design something with GreenSpace Collective
Actually, could this lead to a Knowledge Transfer Partnership?

cost_benefit.title: Strengthening the Case
cost_benefit.narrative:
Your Health Economics colleague helps produce a cost-benefit analysis showing that every ÃÂÃÂ£1 invested in community-led green spaces generates ÃÂÃÂ£3.20 in health and social benefits.

The DPH's eyes light up: "THIS is what I can take to cabinet. They don't understand wellbeing scores, but they understand return on investment."

The council commits ÃÂÃÂ£500,000 to a new Community Green Space Programme, explicitly citing your research and the cost-benefit analysis in the cabinet paper.

This is major policy impact with clear evidence.

choices.text: Secure copies of the cabinet paper and decision documents
Offer to evaluate the new programme  -  creating a research cycle

stay_focused.title: Credibility Preserved
stay_focused.narrative:
You resist the temptation to overreach and focus on what your research actually demonstrates. Your briefing is authoritative, honest about limitations, and includes clear recommendations.

Janet appreciates the integrity: "So many people tell us what they think we want to hear. You've told us what the evidence actually says, including the gaps."

Your evidence is incorporated into the council's strategy with a clear acknowledgment. Janet recommends you to colleagues in two neighbouring councils facing similar challenges.

choices.text: Engage with the neighbouring councils to extend your reach
Apply for funding to address the evidence gaps Janet identified

bold_recommendation.title: Fortune Favours the Bold
bold_recommendation.narrative:
The DPH pushes back initially: "Community-led? We can't just hand over money without accountability."

But you're prepared. You present your evidence showing community-led approaches have better outcomes AND better cost-effectiveness than top-down provision. You share the GreenSpace Collective's data.

Three months later, the council announces a ÃÂÃÂ£300,000 Community Green Space Fund  -  ring-fenced for community organisations in deprived wards. Your research is cited as the evidence base.

Local headlines read: "Council backs community green spaces after university research."

choices.text: Document everything  -  cabinet papers, press coverage, the funding decision

pilot_project.title: Testing the Waters
pilot_project.narrative:
The DPH likes the pilot idea. It's lower risk and produces fresh evidence. The council agrees to fund a 12-month pilot in one ward, with your team providing the evaluation framework.

The pilot is a success. Participants show significant improvements in wellbeing, and the community group running it demonstrates it can be delivered cost-effectively.

The DPH uses the pilot results to secure full council funding for a borough-wide rollout. Your pilot has become a programme.

choices.text: This is perfect  -  document the pilot-to-programme journey as your impact narrative

tailored_briefing.title: Delivering Value
tailored_briefing.narrative:
You produce a superb evidence briefing that directly addresses Janet's three questions. For the cost-effectiveness question, your Health Economics colleague contributes a preliminary analysis.

The briefing lands perfectly. Janet circulates it to the senior leadership team. Three weeks later, you're invited to present to the council's Health & Wellbeing Board.

Your research is directly shaping how the council allocates its green space budget. This is exactly the kind of impact REF panels look for.

choices.text: Present to the Board and secure documentary evidence of influence

advisory_panel.title: Embedded Influence
advisory_panel.narrative:
You join the advisory panel. Over 18 months, your research shapes multiple council decisions about green space investment and design. You keep meticulous records of meetings, recommendations made, and actions taken.

The council's Green Space Action Plan explicitly acknowledges your advisory role and cites your research 14 times. The plan redirects ÃÂÃÂ£2 million in capital spending toward community-led projects.

Sam is delighted: "This is textbook policy impact. You've got the evidence trail, the policy documents, the scale  -  this could be a flagship case study."

choices.text: Compile the impact case study with Sam's help

evidence_letter.title: Building the Evidence Base
evidence_letter.narrative:
You request a formal letter from the council's Director of Public Health confirming how your research influenced their strategy. The letter is specific and powerful, citing exact recommendations that were adopted.

Sam helps you file this alongside the consultation documents, the strategy itself (with your research cited), and the before/after comparison showing what changed.

"This is solid evidential gold," Sam says. "A REF panel wants to see exactly this kind of documentary evidence  -  third-party confirmation of your research's influence."

choices.text: Continue building the case  -  what other evidence should we gather?

strong_evidence.title: The Evidence Portfolio
strong_evidence.narrative:
You systematically build an evidence portfolio:

* Testimonial letters from partner organisations describing specific changes
* Before/after data showing improved outcomes
* The wellbeing toolkit (or funding letter, or programme evaluation) as tangible outputs
* Records of adoption by other organisations
* Independent evaluation data

Sam reviews it all: "This is excellent. You've got corroborated evidence from multiple sources, showing a clear causal chain from your research to real-world change. This is exactly what makes a strong impact case study."

choices.text: Write up the impact case study

track_adoption.title: Measuring Spread
track_adoption.narrative:
You create a simple tracking system for toolkit adoption. Within a year:

* 12 community organisations across the region are using your toolkit
* Two national charities have incorporated it into their evaluation frameworks
* A local authority in another city has adopted it as standard practice

The reach is impressive and growing. Each adopter provides another piece of evidence for your impact case study. Sam helps you map this adoption, showing the "ripple effect" from your original research.

choices.text: Document the full adoption story for the impact case study

scale_up.title: Going National
scale_up.narrative:
You secure UKRI follow-on funding to scale the toolkit nationally, partnering with a network of community organisations. The project reaches 50+ organisations across England.

A national evaluation shows the toolkit is improving how community groups measure and communicate their impact, leading to more successful funding bids and better-targeted services.

Your original research has catalysed a national movement in evidence-based community green space practice.

choices.text: This is a landmark impact story  -  write it up

national_framework.title: Systemic Change
national_framework.narrative:
You co-develop GreenFutures' new evaluation framework. It's adopted as standard practice across their ÃÂÃÂ£10 million annual grants portfolio, meaning every project they fund is now assessed using criteria derived from your research.

This is systemic impact  -  your research has changed how an entire sector operates. The framework is subsequently picked up by two other national funders.

Sam is thrilled: "National reach, multiple beneficiaries, clear evidence of change in practice. This is REF gold."

choices.text: Compile the impact case study

dual_track.title: Balancing Act
dual_track.narrative:
You manage to maintain both the national charity work and local community partnerships  -  but only because you get a part-time research assistant funded through the university's Impact Acceleration Account.

The two tracks complement each other: local partners provide authentic stories and ground-level evidence, while the national work provides reach and systemic change.

After two years, you have an impact story that works at both local and national scale.

choices.text: Write the impact case study  -  you've got a compelling dual narrative

embedded_research.title: A Virtuous Cycle
embedded_research.narrative:
You negotiate a research partnership within the funded project. This means you can track outcomes in real-time, co-produce knowledge with the community, and generate new research outputs.

The funded project delivers excellent results. Your embedded evaluation provides new evidence that feeds into your next publication AND strengthens the impact evidence for REF.

You've created a virtuous cycle: research -> impact -> new research -> greater impact.

choices.text: Document this as your impact case study  -  it's a powerful narrative

ktp_idea.title: Thinking Bigger
ktp_idea.narrative:
A Knowledge Transfer Partnership could place a dedicated associate at GreenSpace Collective, embedding your research into their practice over two years. Sam loves the idea and helps you scope it.

The KTP application is successful. Over 24 months, the associate transforms how GreenSpace Collective operates  -  implementing evidence-based programme design, robust outcomes measurement, and a sustainability strategy.

The Collective grows from 3 sites to 8, secures three major grants, and becomes a national exemplar of evidence-based community practice. All grounded in your research.

choices.text: This KTP story IS the impact case study  -  write it up

conference_impact.title: Amplifying the Story
conference_impact.narrative:
Park Life presents at a national community health conference to 200 delegates. Their presentation  -  co-authored with you  -  shows the before/after transformation with compelling data and participant stories.

Three other organisations approach Park Life to learn how they redesigned their programme. A public health commissioner in the audience asks for your contact details.

The ripple effect is growing. Your research is travelling through practitioner networks in ways you couldn't achieve through academic channels alone.

choices.text: Document this spreading influence for the impact case study

regional_impact.title: Spreading Influence
regional_impact.narrative:
You engage with the two neighbouring councils. Both adopt elements of your evidence into their own green space strategies. One commissions you to conduct a local evaluation.

Your impact has spread across three local authority areas, reaching a combined population of over 500,000. Each council provides documentary evidence of how your research influenced their decisions.

The regional story is compelling: one piece of research, multiple policy changes, growing community benefit.

choices.text: Write the impact case study  -  you've got a strong regional narrative

new_research.title: The Research Cycle Continues
new_research.narrative:
You secure funding to address the evidence gaps Janet identified. This new research, grounded in real policy needs, produces findings that are immediately useful to practitioners and policymakers.

Your reputation as a researcher who produces actionable, policy-relevant evidence grows. More councils and organisations seek your input.

Sam observes: "You've built something rare  -  a genuine, ongoing relationship between research and practice. The REF impact case study almost writes itself."

choices.text: Write up the full impact story

foi_route.title: The Paper Trail
foi_route.narrative:
The FOI response reveals internal council documents showing your consultation response was flagged as "key evidence" and directly informed two of the strategy's priority actions.

This is strong documentary evidence  -  you can show, in the council's own words, that your research shaped their strategy.

Sam nods: "FOI responses are underused as impact evidence. This is the council confirming your influence in their own internal documents. A REF panel will love this."

choices.text: Add this to the evidence portfolio and finalise the case study

ending_policy_star.title: Impact Case Study: Policy Influencer
ending_policy_star.narrative:
Congratulations! You've developed a strong policy-focused impact case study.

Your research journey shows a clear pathway from academic publication to real-world policy change. You built relationships with decision-makers, engaged at the right time, provided evidence in the right format, and documented everything.

Key lessons from your journey:
* Strategy matters  -  random outreach rarely works
* Listen to what stakeholders need, don't just broadcast your findings
* Timing is everything in policy engagement
* Evidence of impact needs to be gathered AS YOU GO, not retrofitted
* Your Impact Officer is your best friend in this process

ending_practitioner_star.title: Impact Case Study: Practice Transformer
ending_practitioner_star.narrative:
Congratulations! You've developed a compelling practice-based impact case study.

Your research has genuinely changed how organisations work, leading to better outcomes for communities. You co-produced knowledge with partners, embedded your research into real-world practice, and built evidence of transformative change.

Key lessons from your journey:
* Co-production with partners creates the strongest impact
* Deep partnerships beat shallow ones
* Let practitioners lead  -  your research supports their expertise
* Tangible outputs (toolkits, frameworks, redesigned programmes) are powerful evidence
* Impact takes time  -  invest in relationships

ending_full_circle.title: Impact Case Study: The Virtuous Cycle
ending_full_circle.narrative:
Congratulations! You've achieved something remarkable  -  a self-sustaining cycle where research drives impact, and impact drives new research.

Your impact case study shows research that didn't just change the world once  -  it created an ongoing relationship between evidence and practice that continues to generate benefits.

Key lessons from your journey:
* The best impact isn't a one-off event  -  it's an ongoing relationship
* Evaluation of your impact can generate new research questions
* Follow-on funding can amplify your original investment
* Building trust with partners creates opportunities you can't plan for
* Impact and research quality reinforce each other

ah_start.title: The Missing Definition
ah_start.narrative:
You're a researcher at Northumbria University. Your team  -  spanning Psychology, Environmental Health, and Nursing  -  has just published the first systematic study of animal hoarding cases in England, in the journal Frontiers in Public Health.

The findings are striking. You identified 66 cases between 2015 and 2020. Cats and dogs were the most commonly hoarded species, appearing in over 60% of cases. The mean was 44 animals per case. Dead animals or animals requiring euthanasia were found in 53% of cases. And perhaps most troublingly, evidence of recidivism  -  repeat hoarding after prosecution  -  was found in 39% of cases.

Your geospatial analysis revealed that cases clustered in urban, densely populated areas with high levels of deprivation.

The clock is ticking toward REF 2029. What you do next will determine whether this research changes policy  -  or gathers dust.

choices.text: Meet with the Impact Officer to develop a stakeholder engagement strategy

ah_strategy.title: Mapping the Landscape
ah_strategy.narrative:
You sit down with the Impact Officer. Together, you map the stakeholder landscape on a whiteboard. It's more complex than you expected.

Animal hoarding sits at the intersection of multiple domains: animal welfare (RSPCA, local authority animal wardens), public health (environmental health officers, Directors of Public Health), mental health (NHS services, hoarding support groups), housing (local authority housing teams), and policy (Defra, the APPG on Animal Welfare  -  APGAW).

"You can't do everything at once," the Impact Officer says. "Where do you want to start?"

choices.text: Build relationships with the APPG  -  they have the power to recommend legislative change
Engage practitioners first  -  the environmental health officers and RSPCA inspectors on the frontline
Convene a multi-agency working group through the UK Hoarding Partnership

ah_direct_appg.title: A Cold Email to Parliament
ah_direct_appg.narrative:
You spend an evening crafting a detailed email to the APPG on Animal Welfare secretariat. You outline your research, attach the Frontiers in Public Health paper, and offer to present at their next evidence session.

Two weeks pass. Three weeks. Then a polite reply arrives: "Thank you for sharing your research. The group receives many submissions and we'll keep your work on file for future reference."

The good news: they now know your name and your research area. The bad news: "on file" often means "in a drawer." You need a different route into the room.

choices.text: Step back and develop a proper strategy with the Impact Officer
Ask the UK Hoarding Partnership network to make a warm introduction
Build your profile through media engagement so they come to you

ah_more_papers.title: Back to the Research
ah_more_papers.narrative:
You decide the evidence base needs strengthening before engaging with policy. Over the next eighteen months, your team publishes two more papers. The first is a qualitative study of RSPCA inspectors' experiences attending animal hoarding cases  -  their frustrations, the emotional toll, and the systemic gaps they face. The second explores barriers to help-seeking among people who hoard animals, drawing on interviews with mental health professionals.

Lesson learned: evidence is necessary but not sufficient. Timing and engagement matter just as much.

choices.text: Use the new publications to approach the APPG about the next inquiry cycle
Build a practitioner network so you're positioned when the next window opens
Try a media strategy to raise public awareness of the issue

ah_media_first.title: Making Headlines
ah_media_first.narrative:
You write an article for The Conversation: "The UK has no legal definition of animal hoarding  -  and that's a problem." The piece uses your research data to paint a vivid picture of the issue: 44 animals per case, dead animals in over half of cases, and a 39% recidivism rate.

The article is picked up by a national newspaper. A regional TV news programme calls asking for an interview. Suddenly your research is getting attention beyond academia.

Media attention has opened doors that a cold email couldn't. But you need to be strategic about which door to walk through.

choices.text: Follow up with the parliamentary researcher immediately
Build the RSPCA relationship first  -  they have permanent parliamentary contacts
Keep the media momentum going  -  more coverage means more pressure for change

ah_appg_relationship.title: Getting Into the Room
ah_appg_relationship.narrative:
Through a combination of your UK Hoarding Partnership connections and the interest generated by your research profile, you secure an introduction to the APPG on Animal Welfare secretariat.

You prepare a two-page policy brief  -  concise, evidence-based, and focused on three key messages:

1. Animal hoarding is a distinct, recognisable pattern  -  not just "having too many pets"
2. The UK has no legal definition, creating a dangerous gap in multi-agency responses
3.

How do you approach the session?

Combine data with anonymised case studies and practitioner testimony
Co-present with an RSPCA inspector who deals with these cases on the ground

ah_practitioners.title: Voices from the Frontline
ah_practitioners.narrative:
You organise a practitioner roundtable at Northumbria's city campus. The room brings together people who rarely sit around the same table: environmental health officers, RSPCA inspectors, social workers, housing officers, and a mental health professional who specialises in hoarding.

Their stories confirm and extend your quantitative findings. An environmental health officer describes entering a terraced house with over 100 cats: "The ammonia hit you before you opened the door. But there's no protocol for this.

What do you do with this practitioner engagement?

choices.text: Write a co-produced report with practitioners and submit it to the APPG
Develop a multi-agency response framework based on what you've heard
Invite a practitioner to co-author your next academic paper

ah_working_group.title: Herding Cats (Metaphorically)
ah_working_group.narrative:
Through the UK Hoarding Partnership, you try to convene a multi-agency working group on animal hoarding. The principle is sound  -  you need everyone around the same table.

But the reality is messy. It takes three months to find a date that works for even half the invitees.

You realise you tried to build the coalition before establishing a clear, shared purpose. People will turn up for a conversation that has a clear proposition and a realistic goal  -  not for an open-ended talking shop.

choices.text: Scale back  -  build bilateral relationships with two or three key stakeholders first
Produce a clear position paper that gives the group a concrete purpose and goal
Focus on the APPG route instead  -  parliament can mandate the coordination you need

ah_ukhp_intro.title: The Warm Introduction
ah_ukhp_intro.narrative:
As Chair of the UK Hoarding Partnership, your colleague has years of established relationships with policy stakeholders, charity sector leaders, and parliamentary contacts. You ask for an introduction to the APPG on Animal Welfare.

The difference from your cold email is night and day. Your colleague frames the introduction carefully: "

This is the power of warm introductions and established networks. Your research opens the door, but trusted relationships get you through it.

Bring in the RSPCA as a co-submitter to strengthen the case

ah_rspca_partner.title: A Powerful Ally
ah_rspca_partner.narrative:
You approach the RSPCA's policy team. They're immediately interested  -  animal hoarding is a persistent operational challenge for their inspectors, and they've been looking for robust research to support their advocacy.

The RSPCA brings something your university can't: a permanent parliamentary affairs team, media infrastructure, and the public's trust.

The partnership is genuine and mutually beneficial. But you need to decide how to deploy it.

choices.text: Submit the joint position to the APPG and request an oral evidence slot
Launch it publicly at a joint press event to build public awareness first
Share it with Defra officials through the RSPCA's existing government contacts

ah_media_campaign.title: Into the Public Eye
ah_media_campaign.narrative:
You and your partners launch a coordinated media campaign. The RSPCA's press office pitches the story; you provide the academic credibility. The angle: "UK law doesn't recognise animal hoarding  -  here's why that matters."

A national newspaper runs a feature. Radio 4's You and Yours covers the issue. A regional BBC news programme films a piece at Northumbria, interviewing you alongside an RSPCA inspector.

Meanwhile, an animal welfare charity asks if you'd contribute to their policy manifesto ahead of the next election.

choices.text: Engage the MP  -  individual parliamentarians can table questions and push for action
Contribute to the charity's manifesto  -  this plants seeds for future government policy
Use the momentum to approach the APPG formally  -  you now have public backing

ah_data_presentation.title: Death by Statistics
ah_data_presentation.narrative:
You present a thorough, data-led session to the APPG. Prevalence rates, geospatial analysis, recidivism statistics, demographic breakdowns, species distribution, deprivation indices.

The parliamentarians are polite. Some take notes. But when you reach the methodology slide, attention drifts. A backbencher checks their phone. The Chair looks at the clock.

Your data is cited in the APPG's subsequent notes, but you're not invited back for the recommendation-drafting stage. You need to find another way to influence the final report.

choices.text: Follow up with practitioner case studies and request another slot
Submit detailed written evidence with case narratives alongside the data
Pivot to developing a practical framework the APPG can include in their recommendations

ah_case_studies.title: Making It Real
ah_case_studies.narrative:
You present the data framed by anonymised but vivid case studies. You open with the numbers  -  66 cases, 44 animals on average, 39% recidivism  -  then bring them to life.

Case 14: A woman in her fifties, living alone in a terraced house in the North West. Environmental health were called after neighbours reported a persistent smell. Officers found 47 cats, 12 of which were dead. The woman was prosecuted, the surviving cats rehomed.

The APPG asks if you'd be willing to contribute directly to their report recommendations.

choices.text: Draft specific policy recommendations focused on a legal definition
Propose a comprehensive multi-agency response framework alongside the definition
Recommend a pilot programme linking prosecution with mental health support

ah_co_present.title: The Researcher and the Inspector
ah_co_present.narrative:
You co-present with an experienced RSPCA inspector who has attended dozens of animal hoarding cases over a fifteen-year career. You provide the research context; they provide the operational reality.

The combination is devastating. Your data shows a 39% recidivism rate; the inspector describes attending the same property three times over five years.

You're invited to contribute to the APPG's draft report.

choices.text: Focus the recommendations on establishing a legal definition of animal hoarding
Recommend a multi-agency framework alongside the definition
Propose a research-informed pilot programme that combines enforcement with support

ah_position_paper.title: Giving the Group a Purpose
ah_position_paper.narrative:
Before trying to reconvene the multi-agency group, you produce a clear position paper through the UK Hoarding Partnership. It's titled: "Animal Hoarding in England: The Case for a Coordinated Response."

The paper sets out three concrete goals the group would work toward:
1. An agreed working definition of animal hoarding for UK use
2. A multi-agency referral and response protocol
3.

The position paper also attracts attention beyond the group. A local authority Director of Public Health shares it with colleagues across the region.

choices.text: Use the group to develop the multi-agency framework collaboratively
Submit the position paper to the APPG as a basis for recommendations
Pursue the DPH connection  -  public health framing could be powerful

ah_joint_report.title: A Unified Voice
ah_joint_report.narrative:
You co-produce a report with practitioners: "No Definition, No Response: The Case for Recognising Animal Hoarding in UK Law."

The report combines your quantitative evidence  -  the 66 cases, the demographic patterns, the recidivism data  -  with qualitative testimony from environmental health officers, RSPCA inspectors, and housing professionals.

Then a Defra policy official contacts you asking for more information. "We're reviewing animal welfare enforcement frameworks," they write. "Your report raises issues we hadn't fully considered."

choices.text: Pursue the Defra connection  -  they're the department that writes animal welfare legislation
Push for the APPG to formally recommend a legal definition in their next report
Develop the practitioner network into a sustainable community of practice

ah_co_author.title: Research as Partnership
ah_co_author.narrative:
You invite a senior RSPCA inspector and an environmental health officer to co-author your next paper. It takes longer than a solo publication  -  your co-authors aren't used to academic writing conventions, and you spend time translating between operational language and research methodology.

But the result is genuinely richer. The paper is published in a public health journal and has credibility with both academics and practitioners because it's authentically co-produced.

Your co-authors become advocates for your research in their own professional worlds  -  amplifying its reach in ways you couldn't achieve from a university office.

choices.text: Use the paper and its practitioner networks to approach the APPG
Develop the co-production approach into a multi-agency framework
Build on this to develop a practitioner-facing toolkit

ah_written_evidence.title: Putting It in Writing
ah_written_evidence.narrative:
You submit comprehensive written evidence to the APPG, weaving together your quantitative data with powerful anonymised case narratives. The document runs to twelve pages, carefully structured to lead with the problem, present the evidence, and close with specific recommendations.

The APPG secretariat confirms receipt and notes that your submission will be circulated to all group members ahead of their next meeting.

But citations are not yet impact. The recommendations need to lead somewhere.

choices.text: Engage with Defra to translate the APPG recommendations into policy action
Develop a practical framework that shows how the recommendations could be implemented
Build a broader coalition to maintain pressure for change

ah_mp_engage.title: A Parliamentary Champion
ah_mp_engage.narrative:
You meet with the MP who contacted you. They represent a constituency with several reported animal hoarding cases, and their casework team has seen the impact firsthand.

The MP tables a written parliamentary question to Defra: "What assessment the Department has made of the adequacy of the current legal framework for addressing animal hoarding in England?" Defra's response is carefully worded but acknowledges that "animal hoarding presents complex, multi-agency challenges."

The MP asks what concrete next step they could support.

choices.text: Ask them to request a Defra review of how animal hoarding is defined and managed
Suggest they host a roundtable in Parliament bringing together all the key stakeholders
Ask them to support a Private Member's Bill or amendment to the Animal Welfare Act

ah_manifesto.title: Seeds for the Future
ah_manifesto.narrative:
You contribute a section on animal hoarding to the charity's animal welfare manifesto. Your research provides the evidence base; they frame it as a call to action for the next government.

The manifesto is published and shared widely among animal welfare organisations, parliamentary candidates, and policy networks.

Meanwhile, the issue is now firmly on the radar of multiple organisations. You've helped shift animal hoarding from an obscure academic topic to a recognised policy gap.

choices.text: Keep building momentum through the APPG and parliamentary engagement
Focus on developing a practical framework so you have a ready-made solution when the political will arrives
Expand the research programme to provide even stronger evidence for the next policy window
Play the long game  -  build impact across policy, practice, and public awareness simultaneously

ah_defra_early.title: Going to the Source
ah_defra_early.narrative:
Through the RSPCA's government affairs contacts, you secure an informal briefing with Defra policy officials. They're interested  -  animal hoarding has been flagged in several recent enforcement reviews  -  but they're also cautious.

There's a recognition that the current framework has gaps," one official tells you. But any legislative change requires a robust evidence base, cross-departmental support, and ministerial interest.

This is useful intelligence. Defra won't act on research alone. You need a broader coalition.

choices.text: Build the practitioner coalition Defra is asking for
Use media to demonstrate public interest in the issue
Engage the APPG to create parliamentary pressure alongside the evidence

ah_public_health.title: The Public Health Angle
ah_public_health.narrative:
You reframe your research through a public health lens. Animal hoarding isn't just an animal welfare issue  -  it's a public health emergency. The ammonia from animal waste causes respiratory disease. Zoonotic infections spread in hoarding environments. The person hoarding is often experiencing severe mental ill-health. Neighbours' quality of life is affected.

You present this framing to the regional Director of Public Health network.

You're building impact from the ground up  -  changing practice at local authority level.

choices.text: Document the local authority pilots as evidence of practice change for REF
Use the DPH endorsement to strengthen your case to the APPG
Expand the public health approach into a national framework

ah_framework_dev.title: Building the Framework
ah_framework_dev.narrative:
Drawing on your research, practitioner engagement, and (if you've pursued it) policy conversations, you develop a proposed Multi-Agency Animal Hoarding Response Framework.

The framework is built on four pillars:

ah_pilot_programme.title: Testing the Alternative
ah_pilot_programme.narrative:
You propose a pilot programme to the APPG: instead of prosecution alone, cases identified as animal hoarding would trigger a coordinated response that includes a mental health assessment, support plan, and ongoing monitoring  -  alongside any necessary enforcement action.

The pilot combines enforcement with therapeutic support. Early results are promising  -  the one case of recidivism in the pilot group involved someone who disengaged from the support programme. The five who stayed engaged have not reoffended.

choices.text: Write up the pilot results and submit to the APPG for their report

ah_toolkit.title: Practical Tools for Practitioners
ah_toolkit.narrative:
You develop a practitioner toolkit: "Recognising and Responding to Animal Hoarding: A Guide for Frontline Professionals."

The toolkit includes a screening checklist, a decision flowchart, a referral template, and a brief summary of the research evidence.

Practitioners report it's the first tool they've seen that treats animal hoarding as a distinct pattern rather than a one-off. One says: "For the first time, I had something to show my manager when I said 'this isn't just someone with too many cats  -  this is hoarding.'"

ah_community_of_practice.title: Building a Movement
ah_community_of_practice.narrative:
You establish a Community of Practice on animal hoarding through the UK Hoarding Partnership. It meets quarterly, mixing researchers, practitioners, charity representatives, and policy professionals.

The community becomes self-sustaining. Members share case experiences, discuss emerging challenges, and collectively develop good practice. Your research remains the foundation, but the knowledge is growing through practice.

The question is whether you consolidate this practitioner impact or push for policy change.

Focus on documenting and scaling the practice change

ah_parliamentary_roundtable.title: In the Palace of Westminster
ah_parliamentary_roundtable.narrative:
The MP hosts a roundtable in a committee room at the House of Commons. The guest list includes your research team, RSPCA representatives, environmental health professionals, Defra officials, and three other parliamentarians with an interest in animal welfare.

You present your research. The RSPCA presents their operational data. Practitioners share frontline experiences.

For REF purposes, this is significant  -  you can evidence that your research has directly informed parliamentary activity and prompted governmental consideration.

ah_legislative.title: The Legislative Route
ah_legislative.narrative:
The MP explores legislative options. A full amendment to the Animal Welfare Act would be ambitious  -  it requires government time and cross-party support. But a Private Member's Bill could raise the issue formally even if it doesn't pass immediately.

The MP tables an Early Day Motion calling on the Government to introduce a legal definition of animal hoarding and a coordinated response framework. Forty-three other MPs sign it.

It won't become law on its own, but it creates a formal parliamentary record, demonstrates cross-party support, and puts pressure on Defra.

Your research is cited in the EDM text by name.

choices.text: Use the EDM momentum to press Defra for a formal policy review
Develop the evidence further with a pilot programme
Document this as the policy impact it is

ah_document_pilots.title: Evidence of Change
ah_document_pilots.narrative:
You systematically document the local authority pilots. Before-and-after data shows improved inter-agency communication, faster case resolution, and  -  critically  -  zero recidivism in the pilot areas during the monitoring period.

Practitioners report feeling more confident and better supported. One environmental health officer says: "For the first time, when I attend a hoarding case, I have a pathway to follow rather than making it up as I go."

But you also have an opportunity to scale beyond these pilot areas.

choices.text: Publish the pilot results and push for national adoption of the framework

ah_la_pilot.title: Testing on the Ground
ah_la_pilot.narrative:
Three local authorities agree to pilot your Multi-Agency Animal Hoarding Response Framework. Each adapts it to their local context  -  one is urban, one suburban, one rural  -  which gives you a natural quasi-experimental design.

Over twelve months, the pilot areas handle 14 animal hoarding cases using the new framework. Compared to the previous year, inter-agency referral rates triple, time to case resolution drops by 40%, and mental health assessments are completed in every case (compared to 15% previously).

The evaluation report is ready. Where does it go?

ah_cieh_publish.title: Through the Professional Body
ah_cieh_publish.narrative:
The Chartered Institute of Environmental Health (CIEH) publishes your framework as a practice guidance document. It carries their professional endorsement, which gives it authority with local authority environmental health teams across the country.

The CIEH promotes it through their professional development programme. Your framework becomes a recommended resource for environmental health officers dealing with animal hoarding cases.

Your research has gone from an academic paper to a nationally endorsed practice guide.

ah_defra_engage.title: Inside the Department
ah_defra_engage.narrative:
You build a relationship with Defra's animal welfare policy team. They invite you to present at an internal seminar  -  a rare opportunity to brief the civil servants who write the legislation.

The presentation goes well. Officials ask sharp questions about the evidence base, the cost of inaction, and what a legal definition would actually look like operationally.

Government wheels turn slowly. But you're now on the inside of the policy machine.

ah_training.title: Professionalising the Response
ah_training.narrative:
You develop a certified training programme: "Understanding and Responding to Animal Hoarding." It's accredited through Northumbria University's continuing professional development framework and co-designed with practitioners.

The programme trains environmental health officers, RSPCA inspectors, social workers, and housing officers to recognise animal hoarding, coordinate multi-agency responses, and understand the mental health dimensions.

Your research has become embedded in professional education  -  a powerful and sustainable form of impact.

ah_expanded_research.title: Deepening the Evidence
ah_expanded_research.narrative:
You secure funding for an expanded programme of research. The new studies include a longitudinal follow-up of hoarding cases, an evaluation of different intervention approaches, and an international comparison of how other countries define and manage animal hoarding.

The international comparison is particularly valuable  -  it shows that countries with legal definitions (like parts of the US and Australia) have significantly better multi-agency coordination and lower recidivism.

Your evidence base is now comprehensive. Combined with your practitioner networks and policy relationships, you have everything needed to make a definitive case.

choices.text: Take the full evidence package to Defra and the APPG

ah_expanded_pilot.title: Scaling the Evidence
ah_expanded_pilot.narrative:
With funding from a public health research council, you expand the pilot to twelve local authority areas. The larger sample provides more robust evidence and captures different local contexts  -  urban and rural, northern and southern, affluent and deprived.

The expanded evaluation confirms the pilot results: coordinated multi-agency responses lead to better outcomes across every measure.

Defra officials, who've been watching the pilots, acknowledge that your framework is the most developed evidence-based model for managing animal hoarding in the UK.

choices.text: Push for the framework to become statutory guidance

ah_ending_policy.title: Impact Case Study: The Definition
ah_ending_policy.narrative:
Your sustained engagement with parliament, Defra, and practitioners has paid off. Working with the APPG, you draft a formal recommendation for a UK legal definition of animal hoarding. The definition draws directly from your research: a pattern of accumulating animals beyond the capacity to provide minimum standards of care, characterised by denial of the inability to provide care, and associated with significant risks to human health, animal welfare, and public safety.

Congratulations! You've achieved policy-level impact.

ah_ending_framework.title: Impact Case Study: Changing Practice
ah_ending_framework.narrative:
Your multi-agency framework has been adopted by local authorities across the country. Through the Chartered Institute of Environmental Health, the UK Hoarding Partnership, and your practitioner networks, the framework has become the standard approach to animal hoarding cases.

34 local authorities have formally embedded it in their protocols.

Congratulations! You've built a practice-based impact case study. The law hasn't changed yet  -  but practice has. And in the messy, multi-agency world of animal hoarding, that's where lives are changed: on the doorstep, in the referral, in the conversation between an environmental health officer and a mental health nurse that never used to happen.

ah_ending_longterm.title: Impact Case Study: The Long Game
ah_ending_longterm.narrative:
Your work has seeded change across multiple fronts. The APPG report recommends a definition. Defra is reviewing the framework. Forty-three MPs signed an Early Day Motion citing your research. Local authorities are piloting your multi-agency approach. The RSPCA, CIEH, and Hoarding UK are all using your evidence.

No single moment captures the impact  -  it's the accumulation of evidence, relationships, and engagement over years.

Congratulations! You've played the long game  -  building impact across policy, practice, and public awareness simultaneously. This is the virtuous cycle of research impact: evidence drives engagement, engagement drives change, and change drives the demand for more evidence.

bfr_start.title: The Exercise Paradox
bfr_start.narrative:
You're a researcher at Northumbria University, working in the Aerospace Medicine and Rehabilitation Laboratory. For years, you've been working on Blood Flow Restriction (BFR) research, a technique that uses surgical-grade tourniquet cuffs to partially restrict blood flow to limbs during low-intensity exercise.

The results are remarkable: BFR produces muscle and bone adaptations comparable to high-intensity training, but at a fraction of the load. In clinical rehabilitation, this is transformative, patients who can't tolerate heavy exercise after surgery or injury can still make meaningful gains.

Your work has attracted attention from unexpected quarters.

Your clinic-based technique could work in microgravity. But getting from rehabilitation room to orbit is a massive leap. Where do you start?

bfr_direct_esa.title: Shooting for the Stars
bfr_direct_esa.narrative:
You submit a research proposal to ESA's open call for spaceflight countermeasure research. The proposal is scientifically rigorous. You outline the clinical evidence, the proposed mechanism, and a detailed experimental protocol for testing BFR in simulated microgravity.

The reviewers are interested but identify gaps. "The science is promising," the feedback reads, "but we have concerns about operational feasibility."

The proposal isn't rejected outright, you're encouraged to resubmit with these gaps addressed. But you need partnerships and operational evidence.

bfr_more_evidence.title: Building the Evidence Mountain

You commit to strengthening the evidence base. Over two years, you run three additional clinical trials: one with post-operative knee patients, one with immobilised elderly patients, and one with healthy participants in simulated bed rest (which mimics some effects of spaceflight).

The bed rest study is particularly significant. Six weeks of bed rest with BFR exercise shows significantly less muscle atrophy and bone mineral loss compared to the control group.

Your evidence is gold-standard. But you need to move faster on translation.

bfr_mod.title: Military Precision

You engage with the Ministry of Defence through Northumbria's defence research connections. Their challenge is compelling: soldiers sustain musculoskeletal injuries in environments where full rehabilitation equipment isn't available. Forward operating bases, ships, remote training facilities.

The MOD is impressed. They want to expand the programme. And the dual-use nature of the technology, military and space, makes it attractive to multiple funders.

bfr_sport.title: Match Day Science
bfr_sport.narrative:
You formalise your relationships with Premier League football clubs. Three clubs agree to participate in a structured study of BFR for post-match recovery and ACL rehabilitation. The physiotherapy teams are enthusiastic. They've been using your informal protocols and want the evidence to back up what they're seeing.

The results are compelling. Players using BFR protocols return to full training 15-20% faster after ACL reconstruction. Post-match muscle soreness markers are significantly lower with BFR recovery sessions.

Explore commercial partnerships to bring BFR to grassroots sport and public health
